newsitem.title: INDIA: Budget steps create greater fiscal discipline-RBI.
newsitem.headline: Budget steps create greater fiscal discipline-RBI.

text.p: Steps announced by Indian Finance Minister P.Chidambaram in his 1997/98 budget state on Friday will result in greater fiscal discipline, C. Rangarajan, governor of the Reserve Bank of India said.
"Well I think there are many many things about which one can be happy," he said in a television interview on Star Plus channel.

"From a monetary and financial system point of view I think the phasing out of the system of ad hoc (treasury bill issues to finance the budget deficit) and the introduction of the Ways and Means Advances (WMA) is an important step," he said.
"I think it will bring about greater fiscal discipline and at the same time give greater autonomy to the Reserve Bank," he said.
Asked how the RBI might exercise its greater freedom in pursuing monetary goals, Rangarajan said: "I would really like to see the inflation rate remain between six and seven percent on an average."
Chidambaram announced that India must prepare to move toward capital account convertibility of the rupee and the RBI will set up a committee to oversee the groundwork.

Rangarajan said that India's foreign exchange reserves of close to $20 billion fulfilled one criteria for moving to capital account convertibility but work need to be done in other areas, notably on comparative inflation rates.

"One of the pre-conditions for capital account convertibility is sufficient level of reserves. That condition has been met but there are other conditions that must be met before we can do it," he said.

"I think the control of inflation and difference in price increases between India and other countries must be moderate. When you have very high differentials it becomes very difficult to link the domestic financial system with the external system," he said.
Rangarajan commented that the rupee in real terms, that is adjusted for inflation, had strengthened against other currencies.
"It is quite true that the rupee in real terms has appreciated because the inflation differentials are still there between our country and other countries," he said.
The Indian government's 1997/98 (April-March) borrowing requirement will not put upward pressure on interest rates or squeeze out corporates also seeking to raise funds, he said.
Rangarajan said that given monetary growth of around 16 percent corporate demand for funds should be satisfied.

"In terms of the borrowing programme I think what is envisaged is not very much higher. It is marginally higher than this year. I think we should be able to get the programme through without putting too much pressure on the interest rate," he said.
"I think we will be able to take care of the requirements of the commercial sector as well as the government sector."
